hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31 with free activities, incentives and grand prizes.
hero.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is encouraging readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, themed "Unearth a Story," running through July 31. According to Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen, the program provides free activities, incentives and grand prizes designed to inspire residents to reconnect with reading. To participate, people can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to receive a prize while supplies last. Those who submit their logs also enter an automatic drawing for one of several grand prizes.

The library has created age-appropriate reward options for different groups. Children up to age 4 receive a rubber duck, while kids ages 5 to 11 can choose between a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dinosaur pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults have the option of selecting a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Activity logs can be picked up and returned at any branch location.

Beyond the reading challenge itself, each library branch is hosting special events throughout the summer. These activities range from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. The library is also bringing characters to various locations, including Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character created specifically for this summer's challenge.

The summer reading initiative aligns with educational research showing that such programs help prevent the summer slide, the learning loss that students can experience during extended breaks from school, according to the American Library Association. The challenge welcomes all county residents and library cardholders. For more information about this summer's reading program or to learn about the special events happening at your local branch, residents can visit their nearest Palm Beach County Library location or contact the library system directly.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie distributes $24 million Waste Pro settlement through property tax credits
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the property tax roll rather than mailing checks to residents. The decision allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement resolves years of trash collection problems that began during the pandemic. Resident Kelly Lee recalled neighbors' garbage overflowing on yards when Waste Pro failed to pick up trash. In 2021, both the city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other, with Waste Pro blaming labor shortages and the city arguing breach of contract for substandard service. In April, after the settlement announcement, Mayor Shannon Martin said she wanted to see cash in residents' pockets. Some residents questioned the fairness of the distribution method, particularly for former residents who lived in Port St. Lucie during the service failures but have since moved. Scott Samples with the city said staff collected data and created scenarios to recommend to council, with the goal of remediating the issues and nightmares residents experienced during the Waste Pro service failures.

cards.headline: Martin County could lose $67 million under proposed homestead exemption expansion
cards.body:
A planned expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could significantly impact Martin County's finances if voters approve the amendment in November. According to a Florida Policy Institute analysis, the county stands to lose more than $67 million in revenue. The impact would extend well beyond the local level, with the same study projecting statewide losses of nearly $4.8 billion for local governments.

The proposed changes would particularly affect renters and low-income residents, despite benefiting homeowners. Mike Readling, Executive Director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, reports a growing number of people requesting assistance with rent and utilities, with 95 percent being renters. He expressed concern that the tax reduction would not help the vulnerable populations his organization serves. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said. The housing crisis appears to be intensifying in the county. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis reveals the severity of the rental shortage: only 24 affordable rental units are available for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

When local governments face revenue shortfalls, they typically have limited options, according to attorney John Tolley. They may cut services, use reserve funds, or increase millage rates. If municipalities raise millage rates, homesteaded homeowners would still enjoy the tax break, meaning they would be largely insulated from the increases. However, landlords who do not qualify for the homestead exemption could see their property tax bills rise. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged this potential chain reaction: "There could be an effect where we see some people getting priced out of these rentals, which are already pretty high." Some property experts, however, see potential benefits in the amendment. The proposal would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartments, from 10 percent to 5 percent. Tolley suggested this reduction might eventually lead to lower rents. Caputo believes municipalities may not raise millage rates at all and argued that market forces could stabilize costs regardless. "If they're paying more for their property, they're going to try and increase that on the tenant and give it a try," Caputo said. "If it doesn't happen for them, then they'll have to readjust their pricing."

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via property tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the property tax roll rather than mailing checks to residents. The decision allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement concludes years of trash troubles in Port St. Lucie. In 2021, both the city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard of service. Resident Kelly Lee attended Monday's meeting and raised questions about fair distribution, noting that some residents who experienced the service problems have since moved while new residents who did not deal with Waste Pro now live in those properties. Scott Samples with the city said staff had been working to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to city council, with the goal of making the best decision possible and helping remediate issues from the Waste Pro era. Mayor Shannon Martin said in April after the settlement announcement that she was committed to making sure residents got paid back for what they dealt with during that time.

cards.headline: Martin County could lose $67 million under proposed Florida homestead exemption expansion
cards.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could cost Martin County more than $67 million in revenue, with critics warning renters may face higher costs if local governments raise tax rates to offset the loss.
cards.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could deliver tax savings to homeowners while potentially burdening renters, according to recent analysis and local experts. The Florida Policy Institute estimates Martin County would lose more than $67 million in local government revenue if voters approve the amendment in November. Statewide, the same study projects local governments could lose nearly $4.8 billion.

The concern is particularly acute for renters, who make up the majority of people struggling with housing costs. Mike Readling, executive director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, reports that 95% of people seeking assistance with rent and bills are renters who would receive no direct benefit from the homestead exemption expansion. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday," Readling said. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis underscores the rental market challenge, finding only 24 affordable and available rental units exist for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

Attorney John Tolley outlined the difficult choices facing local governments confronted with revenue shortfalls. They could reduce services, deplete financial reserves, or increase millage rates. While homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax break even if rates rise, landlords without the exemption would face higher tax bills and might pass those costs to renters. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged this risk but offered a counterargument. "It shouldn't affect them whatsoever," Caputo said of homesteaded homeowners, though he noted landlords "are just going to have a flow through effect, you know, if they're paying more for their property, they're going to try and increase that on the tenant."

The amendment includes a second provision that could influence rental costs. It would lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartment complexes, from 10% to 5%. Tolley suggested this reduction might actually decrease rents. Caputo added that municipalities might not raise millage rates at all, and market forces could prevent significant rent increases. "If it doesn't happen for them, then they'll have to readjust their pricing," Caputo said, noting that rental costs are movable as supply and demand fluctuate. Despite these potential offsetting factors, the immediate question remains whether local governments will cut services, use reserves, or raise rates to fill the projected revenue gap.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach teen Christopher Cetoute killed in North Congress Avenue crash
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute, 14, was fatally struck Friday night while crossing the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue. Police say the driver was speeding and the teen was not using a crosswalk.
cards.body:
Christopher Cetoute, a 14-year-old Congress Middle School student, was fatally struck by a speeding driver Friday night along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. Boynton Beach Police say Christopher was crossing the roadway in an eastbound direction when he was hit by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Police believe speeding played a factor in the crash. Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk and was pronounced dead at the scene. No charges have been filed against the driver at this time.

Friends remember Christopher as loyal, hilarious, determined, caring, and sweet. Abrionna Lang, a close friend, said Christopher attended Congress Middle School and loved playing basketball and track. "He was always easy to get close to," Lang said. She described learning of his death: "At first I didn't believe it until I'd seen a lot of stuff and then I just started crying. Like I was crying for the whole day." The crash has also affected nearby residents. Caurline Robinson, who lives in the area, lost her 5-year-old great-grandchild to a speeding driver in 2021. Robinson said she has witnessed at least seven crashes along Congress Avenue in the last eight years and is calling for safety enhancements. A vigil will be held Friday at 7 p.m. at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue.

cards.headline: Florida university faculty donations tilt heavily Democratic, raising viewpoint diversity concerns
cards.body:
Faculty and staff at Florida's five largest public universities donated nearly nine of every 10 dollars to Democratic candidates and committees during the 2024 federal election cycle, according to an analysis of Federal Election Commission data. The study examined contributions from Florida International University, Florida State University, the University of Central Florida, the University of Florida and the University of South Florida.

The Democratic share of individual donations ranged from 71% at FIU to 89% at UCF. At every school, more than 80% of donors who clearly favored one party directed their contributions to Democrats. By dollar amount, faculty and staff donated to Democratic committees at more than twice the rate of Florida donors generally and directed money to Democrats at roughly four-and-a-half times the rate of their fellow Floridians. These patterns did not resemble the surrounding state.

Ryan Owens, director of the Institute for Governance and Civics at FSU, said the concern is not any individual professor but the overall campus climate. When a campus tilts heavily in one direction, the range of ideas it can test and challenge narrows, often without anyone intending it. A recent Yale committee report on trust in higher education concluded that echo chambers do not produce the best teaching, research or scholarship. The analysis has limits. It studied only the 2024 election cycle and only donations exceeding $200, excluding faculty members who contribute less or do not contribute politically.

Owens said universities can broaden hiring searches to reach qualified scholars whose viewpoints are underrepresented on campus. Departments that have drifted toward intellectual uniformity can become more intentional about recruiting a wider range of perspectives. Institutions can also invest in meaningful civil discourse programs so that students regularly encounter strong arguments from multiple sides and learn to engage with them thoughtfully. Such efforts could complement the civic literacy requirements already expected of Florida students.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom fills food pantry after Facebook post brings community donations
cards.teaser: Jacquelyn Koester operates a Little Free Pantry behind the Hobe Sound Public Library stocked with food and baby essentials for families struggling with rising costs.
cards.body:
Jacquelyn Koester set up a Little Free Pantry outside her Hobe Sound home, located behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, to help neighbors cope with rising food and gas prices. The pantry provides food and baby essentials to anyone in need without questions. After Koester posted on Facebook asking for help keeping the pantry stocked, the community responded with donations. She said the pantry empties faster than she can replace items as prices rise, but the community support has been overwhelming.

The impact of the pantry extends beyond Hobe Sound. One person posted anonymously on the Facebook group saying they drove from Jupiter and the pantry would help them get through the week. Koester said those messages motivate her to maintain the pantry and keep it accessible. She created a Facebook group where residents can learn how to access the pantry and coordinate donations. Koester said villages look different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and want to help.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives toll bills tied to stolen temporary tag
cards.teaser: Vera Keswick-Paine received multiple toll bills for a black Mercedes traveling Florida's Gulf Coast, though she and her husband drive a white Nissan that has had a permanent license plate for months.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast tied to a temporary tag registered to her husband. The bill referenced a black Mercedes and included a photo of the vehicle, but the Keswicks drive a white Nissan that has had a permanent tag for months. Keswick-Paine filed a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police. She expressed concern that the stolen tag could be used for serious crimes, saying if the vehicle ran a red light or was involved in a hit-and-run, the violations would be tied to her husband's name.

Following police advice, Keswick-Paine did not pay the bill and filed a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived anyway. SunPass eventually closed the dispute, but Keswick-Paine said she could not get confirmation the matter was resolved. She received a third toll bill after reaching out in April. The Florida Department of Transportation acknowledged questions from WPTV nearly a month ago but never answered them despite multiple follow-up attempts. Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said temporary tag theft happens frequently, while security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino said the nature of temp tag fraud makes it difficult to investigate. A new Florida law that took effect last year increased penalties for fraudulent use of temp tags and made them easier for the state to track.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents discuss housing concerns at library community event
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library for a Let's Hear It community meetup focused on housing, affordability, and local resources.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to share stories and discuss housing, affordability, local resources, and upcoming events. Much of the conversation centered on affordability and housing challenges. Local activist Delories Butts raised concerns about homelessness in the community, asking why the area cannot help homeless people. Other residents shared their positive experiences living in Belle Glade, with resident Veronica Bain expressing her love for the community.

Residents also learned about available community resources. Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, described an ambassadorship program that selects three students from every school to mentor throughout the year. The program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings, commission meetings, and staying informed about their communities. Holmes explained the organization serves as a voice for people residing in the Glades community. The meetup also highlighted an upcoming historic event: Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, featuring eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. Residents unable to attend monthly Let's Hear It meetups can email LetsHearIt@wptv.com to share their stories and concerns.

cards.headline: Martin County investigates fatal vehicle fire on Citrus Boulevard
cards.teaser: A driver died in a fully engulfed vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court on Saturday night. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle.
cards.body:
Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded Saturday just after 9 p.m. to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. First responders found the driver deceased inside the vehicle, burned beyond recognition. The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire, but detectives ruled out a collision after further investigation at the scene, prompting the Criminal Investigations Division to take over the case.

Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed, with results expected to take several weeks.

hero.headline: Man dies in Martin County vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court
hero.body:
A man died Saturday night in a vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court in Martin County. Deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded just after 9 p.m. to reports of a fully engulfed truck off the side of the road. First responders discovered the driver deceased inside the vehicle, with remains burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially suspected to be a traffic crash-related fire. However, investigators at the scene ruled out a collision as the cause after a thorough examination. The Martin County Sheriff's Office Criminal Investigations Division took over the case and determined the fire likely started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. The driver was unable to escape the burning truck, though the reasons why remain unclear.

Detectives have tentatively identified the victim and have reached out to family members. However, a positive identification cannot be confirmed at this time due to the condition of the remains. DNA testing is underway and expected to take several weeks to complete. The victim's name has not been released pending confirmation through DNA analysis.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office continues its investigation into the circumstances of the fatal vehicle fire as authorities work to determine exactly how the fire started and why the driver could not escape.

cards.headline: 14-year-old Boynton Beach boy killed in North Congress Avenue crash
cards.teaser: Christopher Cetoute of Boynton Beach was struck and killed Friday night while crossing North Congress Avenue in the 4600 block.
cards.body:
A 14-year-old Boynton Beach boy was killed Friday night after being struck by a vehicle while crossing North Congress Avenue, according to the Boynton Beach Police Department. The crash happened just before 9 p.m. on June 12 in the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue. Investigators determined that Christopher Cetoute was crossing the roadway in an eastbound direction when he was hit by a BMW M4 traveling southbound. Police said the vehicle appeared to be traveling at a high rate of speed at the time of the crash. Emergency crews from the Boynton Beach Fire Rescue responded to the scene and pronounced Cetoute dead on site.

Officials said all individuals involved remained at the scene following the crash. Authorities have not released additional details about potential charges or contributing factors. The investigation remains ongoing as detectives work to reconstruct the circumstances leading up to the collision. North Congress Avenue was temporarily impacted as investigators processed the scene late Friday night. The Boynton Beach Police Department is asking anyone with information about the crash to come forward as the case develops.

cards.headline: Friends of Christopher Cetoute mourn Congress Middle School student killed on North Congress Avenue
cards.teaser: A memorial of flowers, a poster and a balloon now stands near the scene where the 14-year-old was fatally struck Friday night in Boynton Beach.
cards.body:
Friends of Christopher Cetoute are mourning the loss of the 14-year-old Congress Middle School student, who was fatally struck by a speeding driver Friday night along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. Christopher was pronounced dead on scene. Boynton Beach Police say he was crossing the roadway going eastbound when he was struck by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Authorities note Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk, and police believe speeding played a factor in the crash. A memorial of flowers, a poster and a balloon now stands near the scene.

Abrionna Lang, a close friend, remembered Christopher as loyal, hilarious, determined, caring and easy to get close to. "To me CC was actually like a best friend," Lang said. The tragedy has also affected nearby resident Caurline Robinson, who lost her 5-year-old great-grandchild to a speeding driver in 2021. Robinson said she has witnessed at least 7 crashes along Congress Avenue in the last 8 years and is calling for safety enhancements. "It's senseless. Where was the urgency to speed? And was it worth taking a life for speed?" she said. No charges have been filed against the driver at this time. A vigil will be held in Christopher's honor Friday at 7pm at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom creates Little Free Pantry to help neighbors with rising food costs
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound resident set up a Little Free Pantry outside her home near the Hobe Sound Public Library to help families struggling with higher food prices.
cards.body:
Jacquelyn Koester established a Little Free Pantry outside her home in Hobe Sound, located behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, to help neighbors cope with rising food and gas prices. Stocked with food and baby essentials, the pantry operates on a no-questions-asked basis for families struggling to afford basic necessities. What began as a simple Facebook post has grown into a steady source of community support. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," Koester said.

After putting out a call for help on Facebook, the community response became overwhelming, with donations regularly filling the shelves. One anonymous Facebook group member posted that they drove up from Jupiter specifically to use the pantry, saying it would help them get through the week. Koester said she knew Hobe Sound would respond because "we are a tight knit community." She credits the continued support to people's willingness to help one another. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," Koester said. For more information on accessing the pantry, visit the Facebook group created by Koester.

cards.headline: Martin County brush fire contained after burning 105 acres near Palm City Newfield neighborhood
cards.teaser: A 105-acre brush fire near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City is now contained after multiple agencies worked together to battle the blaze near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard.
cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office responded to a 105-acre brush fire near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City, located near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard. Residents nearby experienced smoky conditions and increased emergency vehicle activity as crews worked to contain the fire. The smoke and flames were visible from homes in the Newfield neighborhood, drawing crowds of onlookers. Josh Barry, a Newfield resident who recently moved to the neighborhood a few weeks ago, said his wife alerted him to the fire from upstairs. "My wife just started yelling from upstairs, hey there's a fire outside so I ran up and looked and said wow that's really really close," Barry said. He noted that residents lined up from across the neighborhood to watch.

Tom Hornbostel, district chief for Martin County Fire Rescue, explained how the Division of Forestry and Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter operations helped stop the fire's spread. "With their helicopter drops they were able to go by near lakes, pick up water and do what we call water drops to stop the floor progression of the fire," Hornbostel said. Although some neighbors reported seeing ash fall, fire crews said there was no threat to homes or other structures. The fire remains under investigation, but initial clues point to a possible lightning strike from the previous day. Division of Forestry units remained on scene overnight and into Monday morning to monitor for any spot-overs.

Other residents expressed their attachment to the area, with Belle Glade resident Veronica Bain saying "I love it. I love it."

Residents learned about available community resources, including an ambassadorship program run by Glades Lives Matter. Executive director Lavita Holmes explained that the organization takes three students from every school and mentors them throughout the year, holding them civically responsible for attending school board meetings, commission meetings, and staying informed about their communities. Holmes described the program as "a voice for the people that reside in the Glades community." The meetup also featured discussion of upcoming events, including the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, which Codi Snead said currently has eight contestants in grades kindergarten through fifth. Let's Hear It events focus on uncovering the real stories that make communities function.

cards.headline: Boynton Beach redevelopment projects bring housing but threaten Hurricane Alley restaurant
cards.teaser: Two major redevelopment projects are reshaping downtown Boynton Beach, bringing hundreds of apartments and retail space, but Hurricane Alley owner Kim Kelly says her three-decade-old restaurant and 50 employees face an uncertain future.
cards.body:
Two major redevelopment projects are reshaping downtown Boynton Beach, bringing hundreds of apartments and retail space. The Boynton Beach Community Redevelopment Agency is behind both: The Villages, which is already under construction, and The Pierce, a proposed development in the permitting process that would replace several existing properties along the downtown corridor. The Pierce would bring 300 apartments, 17,000 square feet of restaurant, retail, and office space, and 150 public parking spaces. Half of the units will be set aside as workforce housing for at least 15 years, with a portion remaining affordable long-term. The Villages will bring 300 apartments, 8,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space, more than 600 parking spots, and a park.

Standing in the path of The Pierce development is Hurricane Alley, a downtown restaurant that Kim Kelly has owned and operated for three decades. Kelly said she understands the need for redevelopment but wants city leaders to consider what businesses like hers stand to lose. "I understand redevelopment but I also understand taking care of us. Why should we lose our business and lose our jobs because they want to redevelop?" Kelly said. She employs 50 people, and the timeline for any closure remains unclear.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach fire kills 4 dogs, reveals squalid conditions for multiple animals
cards.teaser: A fire at a West Palm Beach property Monday morning killed four dogs and exposed squalid living conditions for multiple animals on the commercial site along the 400 block of 16th Street.
cards.body:
West Palm Beach Fire and Police Departments responded to a fire on Monday morning around 7:05 a.m. along the 400 block of 16th Street. The blaze occurred inside a wooden shed on the commercial property, where several dogs were locked inside at the time. Four dogs died in the fire, and another dog sustained injuries. Further investigation revealed an additional uninjured dog on the property, as well as six cats housed inside a shipping container. All animals on the site were found to be living in squalor.

Animal Care and Control took custody of the surviving animals, and all are expected to recover from their injuries. The West Palm Beach Police Department confirmed that the property was cited on June 11, 2026, by the City of West Palm Beach Code Compliance Division for multiple property maintenance violations.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's deputy gets surprise visit from Vanilla Ice at awards ceremony
hero.teaser: Deputy Tina Izzarone, celebrating 30 years of service, received an unexpected surprise at a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony when rapper Vanilla Ice appeared.
hero.body:
Deputy Tina Izzarone was recognized this month at a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office awards ceremony for 30 years of service. She arrived expecting a standard recognition event, but the occasion held a remarkable surprise. Rob Van Winkle, widely known as the rapper Vanilla Ice, made an unexpected appearance to honor the deputy. "That was amazing," Izzarone said of the moment.

The surprise arrangement came together through a young man named Raffie, who maintained meaningful connections to both the deputy and the celebrity. The connection between Raffie and Izzarone began during a routine traffic stop. When Izzarone pulled over Raffie's mother, she noticed the young man and responded to him with care and attention. "I noticed immediately of his specialness, and I made him feel really at ease knowing that his mother was not in trouble," Izzarone said. Raffie did not forget that kindness. Months later, when their paths crossed again, Raffie approached the deputy and expressed his gratitude. "I see her face and just remembered," Raffie said.

Raffie's longstanding friendship with Van Winkle provided the key to orchestrating the surprise. Van Winkle spoke warmly about his relationship with the young man, saying "Raffie and I go way back when he was a little kid and just a great honor to come out and do this." When Raffie decided to attend the awards ceremony with his mother, he extended an invitation to Van Winkle, who enthusiastically agreed to participate. The rapper described one of their favorite pastimes together, explaining that he owns a large monster truck which Raffie enjoys spending time in during visits. "I have a big monster truck and every time he comes over and every time he comes to my house he says I have to sit in it. Turns the air conditioner on and it's cool," Van Winkle said.

The moment became even more meaningful when an unusual coincidence came to light. Van Winkle and Izzarone share the same birthday on October 31, adding another layer of connection to the surprising encounter. The entire situation developed from a straightforward act of compassion during a traffic stop, demonstrating how simple gestures can create lasting impressions. It should be noted that while Izzarone treated Raffie's mother with consideration during that initial stop, she did issue a ticket for the traffic violation.

cards.headline: Man dies in Martin County vehicle fire off Citrus Boulevard, exhaust may have ignited grass
cards.teaser: A fatal vehicle fire near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court is being investigated as a possible accidental ignition after detectives ruled out a collision as the cause.
cards.body:
A fatal vehicle fire that initially appeared to be the result of a crash is now being investigated as a possible accidental ignition, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. On Saturday, just after 9 p.m., deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to reports of a fully engulfed vehicle off the side of the road near Citrus Boulevard and Pineapple Court. When first responders arrived, they found the driver deceased inside the vehicle. The individual was burned beyond recognition.

The incident was initially treated as a traffic crash-related fire. However, after further investigation at the scene, detectives ruled out a collision as the cause, prompting the involvement of the agency's Criminal Investigations Division. Investigators now believe the fire may have started when the truck's exhaust ignited dry grass beneath the vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the driver was unable to escape the burning truck. Detectives believe they have tentatively identified the victim and have been in contact with family members. However, due to the condition of the remains, a positive identification cannot be made until DNA testing is completed. Those results are expected to take several weeks.

cards.headline: Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach requires adult chaperones for guests 17 and under
cards.teaser: Rapids Water Park has implemented an interim youth supervision policy requiring all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone while visiting the park.
cards.body:
Rapids Water Park in Riviera Beach has implemented an interim youth supervision policy requiring all guests ages 17 and younger to be accompanied by an adult chaperone. According to the park, the policy is part of its ongoing effort to maintain a safe and enjoyable environment for guests at South Florida's largest water park. Minors ages 17 and under must be accompanied by an adult chaperone, defined as a parent, legal guardian or other responsible adult who is at least 21 years old and traveled to the park with the minor's group.

All adult chaperones must present a valid government-issued ID showing both a photograph and date of birth upon entry. Chaperones must be present when their group enters the park and remain on-site for the duration of the visit. Rapids Water Park limits each adult chaperone to supervising no more than 5 guests who are 17 years old or younger per day. Park officials said the measure aligns with the park's commitment to providing a family-friendly destination where guests can safely enjoy its attractions. The youth supervision policy is currently listed as an interim measure and is now in effect.

cards.headline: 105-acre brush fire near Palm City neighborhood contained after lightning strike
cards.teaser: A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County is now contained after multiple agencies worked together to battle the blaze near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City.
cards.body:
A 105-acre brush fire in Martin County near the Newfield neighborhood in Palm City is now contained after multiple agencies responded to the wildfire near Newfield Boulevard and Southwest Citrus Boulevard. Martin County Fire Rescue, the Florida Division of Forestry, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office worked together to battle the blaze. Residents in the area experienced smoky conditions and increased emergency vehicle activity as crews worked to contain the fire. The smoke and flames were visible from homes in the Newfield neighborhood, drawing crowds of onlookers.

Tom Hornbostel, district chief for Martin County Fire Rescue, explained that the Division of Forestry and Martin County Sheriff's Office helicopter operations stopped the fire's spread by picking up water from nearby lakes and making water drops. Although some neighbors reported seeing ash fall, fire crews said there was no threat to homes or other structures. Hornbostel said the fire is still under investigation, but initial clues point to a possible lightning strike from the day before the fire broke out. Division of Forestry units remained on scene overnight and into Monday morning to closely monitor the fire for any spot-overs.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running through July 31. Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen said the program offers free activities, incentives and grand prizes to encourage residents to rediscover the joy of reading. Participants can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to claim a prize while supplies last. Returned logs also qualify readers for a drawing to win one of several grand prizes.

Prizes vary by age group. Little learners up to age 4 can take home a rubber duck. Kids ages 5 to 11 can choose from a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dino pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults can opt for a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Each library branch is hosting special events including children's story times, craft sessions, adult workshops and wellness programs. Families will also see Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character visiting for the challenge, at various appearances. According to the American Library Association, summertime reading programs help prevent the summer slide in student learning. The challenge is open to all county residents and library cardholders.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County Library launches summer reading challenge through July 31
hero.teaser: The Palm Beach County Library System is inviting readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, running now through July 31 with free activities, incentives and grand prizes.
hero.body:
The Palm Beach County Library System is encouraging readers of all ages to participate in its 2026 Summer Reading Challenge, themed "Unearth a Story," running through July 31. According to Community Engagement Manager Lindsey McMullen, the program provides free activities, incentives and grand prizes designed to inspire residents to reconnect with reading. To participate, people can register at any library branch, complete an activity log and return it to receive a prize while supplies last. Those who submit their logs also enter an automatic drawing for one of several grand prizes.

The library has created age-appropriate reward options for different groups. Children up to age 4 receive a rubber duck, while kids ages 5 to 11 can choose between a fidget spinner, dinosaur-themed pop keychain or dinosaur pencil. Teens ages 12 to 17 and adults have the option of selecting a fidget spinner, chip clip or notebook. Activity logs can be picked up and returned at any branch location.

Beyond the reading challenge itself, each library branch is hosting special events throughout the summer. These activities range from children's story times and craft sessions to adult workshops and wellness programs. The library is also bringing characters to various locations, including Dewey the Library Owl and Penelope Rex, a dinosaur character created specifically for this summer's challenge.

The summer reading initiative aligns with educational research showing that such programs help prevent the summer slide, the learning loss that students can experience during extended breaks from school, according to the American Library Association. The challenge welcomes all county residents and library cardholders. For more information about this summer's reading program or to learn about the special events happening at your local branch, residents can visit their nearest Palm Beach County Library location or contact the library system directly.

cards.headline: Smithsonian Marine Exhibit in Fort Pierce offers up-close encounters with Florida ecosystems
cards.teaser: The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St.
cards.body:
The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit at the St. Lucie County Aquarium invites visitors to explore Florida's coastal habitats with rare close-up encounters with marine life in Fort Pierce's waterfront district. Manager Bill Hoffman says the facility's philosophy of displaying fully live, complex models of ecosystems dates back to 1980 under the Smithsonian, making it unlike most public aquariums. "We feel like we're the best kept secret on the Treasure Coast, and we don't want to be," Hoffman told WPTV, noting that more species are housed here than in many larger exhibits. The highlight is the Atlantic coral reef exhibit, a sprawling tank that recreates one of Florida's most significant coastal ecosystems. Visitors will also see live models of seagrass beds, mangroves, and hardbottom communities, each demonstrating intricate relationships between organisms, including the aquarium's barracuda, which measures just four inches.

The exhibit's touch tank is another crowd favorite, according to exhibit educator Chelsie Corcoran, where guests can handle unusual marine species under staff guidance. Upcoming programming will tie into the facility's 25th anniversary celebration later this year. The Smithsonian Marine Ecosystems Exhibit operates in partnership with the Smithsonian Marine Station, aiming to raise public awareness about threats facing oceans while inspiring conservation. The facility is located at 420 Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce and is open to the public year-round. More information can be found at sms.si.edu and on their Smithsonian Marine Station social media channels.

cards.headline: Humane Society of the Treasure Coast thrift stores house cats during Palm City shelter renovation
cards.teaser: The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is using its two Stuart thrift stores to keep animal care going strong during a major renovation of its shelter in Palm City.
cards.body:
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast began construction on its adoption, customer service, and intake areas earlier this year, temporarily shifting many of its cats to its two thrift stores during the Palm City shelter renovation. "With our shelter cages unavailable, the stores have become a lifeline for our animals," spokesperson Sarah Fisher said Thursday. Senior Manager Kelly Ellis said shoppers can now find not only unique items for sale but also adoptable cats at both thrift stores. "Every treasure you find here helps provide for our animals," Ellis noted, adding that donations of gently used goods are welcome.

The organization is currently seeking temporary foster homes for other animals while construction continues. The Humane Society's thrift stores are located at 3302 SE Federal Highway in Stuart and 1099 NW 21st St, Stuart. Store hours and donation guidelines are available at hstc1.org.

hero.headline: Florida university faculty donations tilt heavily Democratic, raising viewpoint diversity concerns
hero.body:
Faculty and staff at Florida's five largest public universities donated nearly nine of every 10 dollars to Democratic candidates and committees during the 2024 federal election cycle, according to an analysis of Federal Election Commission data. The study examined contributions from Florida International University, Florida State University, the University of Central Florida, the University of Florida and the University of South Florida.

The Democratic share of individual donations ranged from 71% at FIU to 89% at UCF. At every school, more than 80% of donors who clearly favored one party directed their contributions to Democrats. By dollar amount, faculty and staff donated to Democratic committees at more than twice the rate of Florida donors generally and directed money to Democrats at roughly four-and-a-half times the rate of their fellow Floridians. These patterns did not resemble the surrounding state.

Ryan Owens, director of the Institute for Governance and Civics at FSU, said the concern is not any individual professor but the overall campus climate. When a campus tilts heavily in one direction, the range of ideas it can test and challenge narrows, often without anyone intending it. A recent Yale committee report on trust in higher education concluded that echo chambers do not produce the best teaching, research or scholarship. The analysis has limits. It studied only the 2024 election cycle and only donations exceeding $200, excluding faculty members who contribute less or do not contribute politically.

Owens said universities can broaden hiring searches to reach qualified scholars whose viewpoints are underrepresented on campus. Departments that have drifted toward intellectual uniformity can become more intentional about recruiting a wider range of perspectives. Institutions can also invest in meaningful civil discourse programs so that students regularly encounter strong arguments from multiple sides and learn to engage with them thoughtfully. Such efforts could complement the civic literacy requirements already expected of Florida students.

cards.headline: Five Pinellas County Commissioners endorse Melissa Rutland for House District 60
cards.teaser: A Republican majority on the Pinellas County Commission has endorsed Melissa Rutland to replace outgoing Democratic Rep. Lindsay Cross in House District 60.
cards.body:
Five of the seven Pinellas County Commissioners are endorsing Melissa Rutland, a Republican seeking to represent House District 60 after Democrat Lindsay Cross announced she would not seek re-election. The endorsers are Dave Eggers, Vince Nowicki, Kathleen Peters, Chris Scherer and Brian Scott. Chris Latvala is the only Republican commissioner who has not offered support, while Rene Flowers, the board's sole Democrat, is unlikely to support Rutland because Democrat Lindsay Polega-Quigley is also running in the race.

Rutland is a small-business owner with deep Pinellas County roots stretching back more than a century. Her family built St. Petersburg's business community through Rutland Brothers Department Store, Rutland's men's store on Central Avenue, and St. Petersburg Bank Trust, which eventually became Rutland Bank. In 2015, she founded the Rutland Florida Gulf Group, specializing in commercial investments. She also was appointed by Mayor Rick Kriseman to the St. Petersburg Development Review Commission in 2015, where she served nearly a decade including a stint as its first female Chair. Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to the Juvenile Welfare Board of Pinellas County. Rutland entered the race last week and does not face primary opposition.

cards.headline: Former Gov. Charlie Crist gains Darryl Rouson endorsement in St. Petersburg mayoral race
cards.teaser: State Sen. Darryl Rouson endorsed former Gov. Charlie Crist for St. Petersburg mayor while maintaining his support for current Mayor Ken Welch, saying both should advance from the Primary.
cards.body:
Darryl Rouson, a highly trusted leader in St. Petersburg's Black community who has been active in local politics for almost 20 years, is backing former Gov. Charlie Crist for mayor while maintaining his support for current Mayor Ken Welch. Rouson said he is unsure who he will vote for but believes "both Ken and Charlie should make it out of the Primary." Rouson was elected to the House in 2008 and to the Senate in 2016. He will leave office this year because of term limits, ending a legislative career of about 18 years. In praising Crist, Rouson said, "I believe Charlie meets the threshold to lead our city" and highlighted Crist's "integrity and dedication to public service."

By supporting both candidates, Rouson sends a message to Black residents who may want to continue supporting the city's first Black Mayor. Welch is almost certain to be a front-runner as the incumbent, while Crist has quickly become the other main contender. New fundraising reports show Crist's political committee, St. Pete Shines, received another $283,000, bringing his total to over $1.6 million. Welch raised less than half that in the latest period, with his committee holding just over $300,000. Welch has faced considerable criticism over his handling of the 2022 hurricanes, the failed Tampa Bay Rays stadium deal, and ongoing water billing problems. The August 18 Primary also includes City Council member Brandi Gabbard, former fire chief Jim Large, prison administrator Maria Scruggs, and former Shore Acres Neighborhood Association President Kevin Batdorf.

cards.headline: Orlando space startup NUVIEW advances Moon mapping mission with European Space Agency
cards.teaser: NUVIEW, an Orlando company backed by Leonardo DiCaprio, won selection for a Phase A study to map the Moon's polar regions using commercial LiDAR technology.
cards.body:
NUVIEW, an Orlando-based space-LiDAR startup co-founded by Clint and Katie Graumann, announced that its Moonraker mission has been selected by the European Space Agency for a Phase A study under ESA's Small Missions for Exploration program. The selection marks the next step following pre-Phase A work that NUVIEW GmbH, the company's German arm, has been leading since late 2024. NUVIEW serves as the prime contractor on an international consortium that includes Canada's SFL Missions and Germany's DLR.

A LiDAR-equipped spacecraft would enter lunar orbit and generate high-resolution, 3D elevation models of the polar regions, including the permanently shadowed craters near the South Pole where future landers will search for water ice. Katie Graumann, CEO of NUVIEW's German entity, said the Moonraker mission represents a direct extension of the company's commercial LiDAR architecture into lunar orbit. By adapting systems deployed for Earth observation, the company can provide reliable terrain data to reduce risk for future lunar landings. Early backers include Florida Funders and Leonardo DiCaprio, who made NUVIEW his first space investment. A target launch date of no earlier than 2028 indicates Phase A remains a study rather than a launch contract.

cards.headline: The Southern Group expands Orlando office with former legislative staffer Julian Cintron
cards.teaser: The Southern Group hired Julian Cintron, an Orlando native and former legislative staffer, to focus on local government advocacy in Central Florida.
cards.body:
The Southern Group is expanding its Central Florida team with the addition of Julian Cintron to the firm's Orlando office. An Orlando native and former legislative staffer, Cintron will focus on local government advocacy, helping clients navigate policy, economic development, land-use and infrastructure issues before city councils, county commissions and regional governing bodies. Rachel Cone, Senior Managing Partner at The Southern Group, said building out the local advocacy bench across the state has been a deliberate focus for the firm. "Julian is exactly the kind of addition we need to help grow our local advocacy practice in Central Florida," Cone said.

Before joining The Southern Group, Cintron worked for Reps. Joy Goff-Marcil, Leonard Spencer and Anna Eskamani, as well as Sens. Carlos Guillermo Smith and Victor Torres. His legislative work included issues such as workforce development, artificial intelligence and transportation innovation. Cintron helped lead Orlando YIMBY, a housing advocacy organization focused on land-use and growth policy issues, and managed Spencer's successful 2024 campaign in House District 45, the only Democratic state House pickup in Florida that cycle. Torres said Cintron "knows how to work this process and build the relationships that get things done," while Eskamani called him "a proven advocate."

cards.headline: President Trump announces largest fireworks show in history for July 4 in Washington
cards.teaser: President Trump will host a Tribute to America rally at the Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument on July 4, featuring military bands and what he described as the largest fireworks show in history.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced he will host a rally on July 4 at the Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument in Washington, D.C. Starting at 7 P.M. EST, the celebration will honor the country's people, spirit, strength, resolve and triumphs. More than 300 members of military bands, orchestras and ceremonial units will perform patriotic melodies and American classics, as well as Trump's playlist. Trump said the ensemble will be the largest formation of Joint Military Music and Ceremonial performances in history.

The event will feature flyovers and airshows featuring top military pilots and equipment. Trump will deliver keynote remarks. To conclude the program and commemorate the occasion, Trump said he will launch what will be the largest fireworks show in history in the nation's capital. Trump said the celebration will be held in beautiful and safe Washington D.C., with the backdrop of the Lincoln Memorial and surrounding the beautifully new Reflecting Pool.

Trump promoted the event as a tribute to America, stating it will rally the country into the next 250 years. He said attendees will not want to miss the keynote remarks and encouraged people to attend on July 4 in Washington, D.C.

hero.headline: Martin County could lose $67 million under proposed homestead exemption expansion
hero.body:
A planned expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could significantly impact Martin County's finances if voters approve the amendment in November. According to a Florida Policy Institute analysis, the county stands to lose more than $67 million in revenue. The impact would extend well beyond the local level, with the same study projecting statewide losses of nearly $4.8 billion for local governments.

The proposed changes would particularly affect renters and low-income residents, despite benefiting homeowners. Mike Readling, Executive Director of Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, reports a growing number of people requesting assistance with rent and utilities, with 95 percent being renters. He expressed concern that the tax reduction would not help the vulnerable populations his organization serves. "The demographic that we're working with and Habitat for Humanity tries to help, it's not going to help them at all," Readling said. The housing crisis appears to be intensifying in the county. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis reveals the severity of the rental shortage: only 24 affordable rental units are available for every 100 extremely low-income renters.

When local governments face revenue shortfalls, they typically have limited options, according to attorney John Tolley. They may cut services, use reserve funds, or increase millage rates. If municipalities raise millage rates, homesteaded homeowners would still enjoy the tax break, meaning they would be largely insulated from the increases. However, landlords who do not qualify for the homestead exemption could see their property tax bills rise. Realtor Michael Caputo acknowledged this potential chain reaction: "There could be an effect where we see some people getting priced out of these rentals, which are already pretty high." Some property experts, however, see potential benefits in the amendment. The proposal would also lower the property tax cap on non-homesteaded properties, including commercial apartments, from 10 percent to 5 percent. Tolley suggested this reduction might eventually lead to lower rents. Caputo believes municipalities may not raise millage rates at all and argued that market forces could stabilize costs regardless. "If they're paying more for their property, they're going to try and increase that on the tenant and give it a try," Caputo said. "If it doesn't happen for them, then they'll have to readjust their pricing."

cards.headline: Hobe Sound mom sets up Little Free Pantry to help families with rising food costs
cards.teaser: A Hobe Sound resident has set up a Little Free Pantry outside her home behind the Hobe Sound Public Library after rising food costs left the pantry emptying faster than she could replace it.
cards.body:
Jacquelyn Koester, a Hobe Sound mom, established a Little Free Pantry located behind the Hobe Sound Public Library to help neighbors cope with rising food costs. The pantry is stocked with food and baby essentials for families struggling with higher prices. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," Koester said. After posting a call for help on Facebook, the community response has been overwhelming, with donations regularly filling the shelves. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," Koester said.

The pantry operates with no questions asked, providing support to anyone in need. One anonymous Facebook user posted that they drove up from Jupiter to access the pantry, saying it would help them get through their week. Koester says messages like these keep her motivated to maintain the pantry and keep it accessible. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," she said. More information on accessing the pantry is available through the Facebook group Koester created.

cards.headline: Charred remains found inside burning truck in Martin County
cards.teaser: A driver was found dead inside a burning vehicle in Martin County on Tuesday morning.
cards.body:
Martin County authorities are investigating after charred remains were found inside a truck that caught fire on Tuesday morning. The driver was pronounced dead on scene.

Details about the location of the fire and the circumstances surrounding the death are under investigation. Multiple agencies responded to extinguish the blaze.

cards.headline: Fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County extinguished by multiple agencies
cards.teaser: A fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County required response from multiple agencies to bring under control.
cards.body:
Multiple fire agencies responded to extinguish a fire near Newfield Parkway in Martin County on Monday evening. The fire was brought under control with assistance from several responding units.

The cause of the fire and extent of any damage are under investigation.

cards.headline: Brush fire briefly slows traffic on I-95 northbound in Palm City
cards.teaser: A brush fire along I-95 northbound in Palm City caused brief traffic delays on Monday evening.
cards.body:
A brush fire on Monday evening briefly slowed traffic on I-95 northbound in Palm City. The fire was extinguished and traffic resumed normal flow.

The cause of the brush fire is under investigation.

cards.headline: Two Martin County restaurants receive perfect inspection scores while three fail
cards.teaser: Two Martin County restaurants earned perfect scores in recent health inspections, while three failed and one was closed.
cards.body:
State health inspectors awarded perfect scores to two Martin County restaurants in recent inspections. Three other restaurants failed their inspections, and one establishment was ordered closed.

The restaurants receiving perfect scores and those that failed were not immediately identified in available reports.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie council votes to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie city council voted to distribute funds from the $24 million Waste Pro settlement through the tax roll rather than sending out checks.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders voted Monday to distribute the $24 million settlement from their former trash hauler Waste Pro via the tax roll rather than sending checks to residents. The decision allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties through an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement followed lawsuits filed by both the city and Waste Pro in 2021. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract regarding service standards. Resident Kelly Lee, who attended the meeting, recalled her neighbors' trash collection problems during the pandemic, describing piled garbage that overflowed in yards. Scott Samples with the city said staff worked to collect data and create scenarios for council recommendations, noting that "ultimately the goal is to make the best decision possible, help remediate some of those issues, and those nightmares that people have from back then." Lee raised concerns about fair distribution, noting that some residents who experienced the service failures have since moved away.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County among Florida's riskiest real estate markets
hero.teaser: St. Lucie County has been identified among the riskiest real estate markets in Florida.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County has been identified as one of Florida's real estate markets facing elevated risk factors. The county joins other Florida communities that are experiencing concerns about their housing and property markets, according to recent analysis of regional real estate conditions.

While specific details about the risk factors were not provided in available reporting, the designation reflects broader challenges affecting the county's real estate sector. Communities across Florida have faced various pressures that impact property values and market stability, and St. Lucie County appears to be among those experiencing these concerns more acutely than some other areas of the state.

The identification of St. Lucie County as a higher-risk market comes as the community continues to address other local challenges. The Port St. Lucie city council recently voted to distribute over 24 million dollars in settlement funds from Waste Pro, the city's former trash hauler, through the property tax roll rather than sending checks directly to residents. The settlement resulted from service failures during the pandemic, when residents experienced significant trash collection issues. City officials chose the tax roll distribution method to provide funds directly to properties through an established system.

The waste service problems that led to the settlement had troubled residents for years. During the pandemic, many property owners faced overflowing trash and missed pickups. The city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other in 2021, with the company citing labor shortages while the city argued the company had breached its service contract. The two parties reached a settlement agreement, with Waste Pro paying 24 million dollars in compensation. The city council's decision to distribute funds via the tax roll allows the city to apply credits to property accounts systematically. Council members also voted against using settlement money to reimburse the city for emergency solid waste expenses incurred during the service failures. City officials noted that staff members had worked extensively to collect data and develop distribution scenarios to present recommendations to the council, with the goal of remedying the issues and frustrations residents experienced during that difficult period.

cards.headline: Film 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' begins shooting in Fort Pierce June 26
cards.teaser: A new film is scheduled to begin production in Fort Pierce later this month, with filming also planned for Rockledge.
cards.body:
The film 'As For Me & My House, Sundays Is For Church' is scheduled to begin filming on June 26 in Fort Pierce. The production will continue on June 27 in Rockledge. The announcement was made Monday.

The Fort Pierce filming date marks the start of the production schedule for the project. Details about the specific locations within Fort Pierce where filming will take place were not provided in the announcement.

cards.headline: Historic tall ship Elissa makes Fort Pierce stop on route to New York celebration

The tall ship Elissa, built in 1877, stopped in Fort Pierce during its voyage to New York for a 250th celebration. The historic vessel made the port call Monday as it traveled along the East Coast.

The ship's stop in Fort Pierce is part of a longer journey that will culminate in New York for the anniversary event. The Elissa is traveling northward along Florida's coast before continuing to its final destination.

cards.body:
A wrongful death lawsuit was filed in St. Lucie County related to a fatal crash on the Florida Turnpike that involved a semi-truck driver. The legal action was filed Monday.

The lawsuit stems from the fatal collision on the Turnpike. The case was filed in St. Lucie County court and involves the semi-truck driver as a defendant in the wrongful death claim.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to distribute $24 million Waste Pro settlement via property tax roll
cards.teaser: Port St.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council voted Monday to distribute $24 million from a settlement with former trash hauler Waste Pro through the property tax roll rather than mailing checks to residents. The decision allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties using an established system. Council members also voted not to reimburse the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund.

The settlement concludes years of trash troubles in Port St. Lucie. In 2021, both the city and Waste Pro filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard of service. Resident Kelly Lee attended Monday's meeting and raised questions about fair distribution, noting that some residents who experienced the service problems have since moved while new residents who did not deal with Waste Pro now live in those properties. Scott Samples with the city said staff had been working to collect data and create scenarios to give recommendations to city council, with the goal of making the best decision possible and helping remediate issues from the Waste Pro era. Mayor Shannon Martin said in April after the settlement announcement that she was committed to making sure residents got paid back for what they dealt with during that time.

cards.headline: Six St. Lucie County restaurants earn perfect inspection scores while four fail
cards.teaser: Recent health inspections in St. Lucie County resulted in six restaurants receiving perfect scores and four failing their inspections.
cards.body:
Six restaurants in St. Lucie County received perfect scores during recent health inspections. Four other restaurants in the county failed their inspections.

The inspection results were released Tuesday. The perfect scores and failures represent the most recent round of health inspections conducted by county officials at St. Lucie County dining establishments.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound mom fills community food pantry as neighbors struggle with rising costs
hero.body:
A Hobe Sound resident is supporting her neighbors during financially difficult times by establishing a Little Free Pantry outside her home. Jacquelyn Koester launched the initiative after posting in a local Facebook group, determined to make sure families in the area could access basic food items and necessities without embarrassment or judgment. What began as a straightforward request for community assistance has evolved into an ongoing resource that serves anyone facing hardship, regardless of their circumstances.

The pantry sits just behind the Hobe Sound Public Library, steps away from Koester's residence. Its shelves hold food and baby essentials intended for families struggling to manage their household budgets as inflation drives up everyday expenses. Koester observed that once fuel and grocery prices climbed, the pantry's contents disappeared much faster than she could replenish them. "When gas prices went up and food prices went up it was just emptying about faster than I can replace it," she explained. Despite the challenge of keeping up with demand, the overwhelming community response has sustained the effort.

After Koester reached out for help on Facebook, neighbors stepped up significantly to keep the pantry stocked. The contributions have been consistent and generous, ensuring the shelves remain filled for those who need them. One person even commented anonymously that they had driven from Jupiter specifically to visit the pantry and that access to its contents would help them survive the week. These messages of gratitude and stories of real impact fuel Koester's commitment to maintaining the resource and making sure it remains accessible to everyone in need.

Koester credits the tight-knit nature of Hobe Sound for the pantry's success. "I knew the second I posted on that group that Hobe Sound was going to show up for us because that's what we do, we are a tight knit community," she said. She reflects on how community support has evolved over time. "The saying it takes a village is so true and the villages look a lot different than they used to, but people still show up for each other and people want to help," Koester said. What now stands outside her home represents far more than a simple pantry. It has become a tangible symbol of neighbors caring for one another during uncertain economic times. Community members interested in supporting the pantry or accessing its resources can find more information through the Facebook group Koester created.
