cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie city leaders voted to distribute the $24 million settlement from former trash hauler Waste Pro via the tax roll rather than sending out checks.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city leaders voted Monday to distribute the $24 million settlement from their former trash hauler Waste Pro via the tax roll rather than sending checks to residents. The tax roll method allows the city to distribute funds directly to properties through an established system.

Council members also voted against reimbursing the city for prior emergency solid waste expenses in the general fund. In 2021, both the company and city filed lawsuits against each other. Waste Pro blamed labor shortages while the city argued the company breached its contract for standard service. The parties reached a settlement agreement with Waste Pro paying $24 million. Mayor Shannon Martin previously told WPTV in April that she was committed to making sure residents get paid back for their experience during that time. Some residents questioned how the distribution would be handled fairly, particularly for former residents who no longer live in the city but dealt with service issues during the pandemic.

cards.headline: Florida homestead exemption expansion could shift tax burden from owners to renters
cards.teaser: A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics warn renters may end up paying the price if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue.
cards.body:
A proposed expansion of Florida's homestead exemption could lower tax bills for homeowners, but critics worry renters may end up paying the price if local governments raise rates to offset lost revenue. A Florida Policy Institute analysis estimates Martin County alone could lose more than $67 million if the amendment passes in November, with local governments statewide potentially losing nearly $4.8 billion. At Habitat for Humanity of Martin County, Executive Director Mike Readling says he's seeing an uptick in people seeking help with rent and bills, 95% of whom are renters. "The housing situation is so dire. It's gotten progressively worse. We have families coming in everyday," Readling said, adding the proposed tax cut would do little for the people his organization serves.

Attorney John Tolley says local governments facing a revenue shortfall could cut services, dip into reserves, or raise millage rates. If millage rates rise, homesteaded homeowners would still benefit from the tax break, according to realtor Michael Caputo. However, landlords who don't receive the exemption could face higher tax bills and potentially pass those costs to renters, who also don't get the tax break. A 2025 Florida Senate analysis found there are just 24 affordable and available rental units for every 100 extremely low-income renters in the state.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Gardens woman receives repeated toll bills tied to stolen temp tag
cards.teaser: A Palm Beach Gardens woman says she cannot get answers from the Florida Department of Transportation after repeatedly receiving toll bills from roads that neither she nor her husband have traveled.
cards.body:
Vera Keswick-Paine of Palm Beach Gardens received a toll bill in March for multiple tolls along Florida's Gulf Coast with a license plate number matching a temporary tag registered to her husband. The bill referenced a black Mercedes with a photograph, but the Keswicks drive a white Nissan with a permanent tag they have had for months. After filing a report with Palm Beach Gardens Police, Keswick-Paine said the situation became more concerning than a bill for under $10. Following police advice, she did not pay and instead filed a dispute with SunPass. A second invoice arrived regardless, and though SunPass eventually closed the dispute, Keswick-Paine could not get confirmation the matter was resolved.

Personal injury attorney Doug Burnetti said the problem is far more common than many realize. Security consultant and retired police officer Gene Petrino said the best way to protect yourself from temp tag theft is to keep thorough records of any police reports and toll disputes. Petrino also recommended destroying temporary tags yourself by cutting them into pieces or surrendering them to the tag agency with your information eliminated. A new law in Florida that took effect last year increased penalties for fraudulent use of temporary tags and made the tags easier for the state to track.

cards.headline: Belle Glade residents share housing concerns, community pride at library event
cards.teaser: More than a dozen Belle Glade residents came to the Belle Glade Library to share their stories during a Let's Hear It community meetup, covering topics from housing and affordability to local resources and upcoming events.
cards.body:
More than a dozen Belle Glade residents gathered at the Belle Glade Library during a Let's Hear It community meetup to discuss housing affordability, local resources, and upcoming events. Much of the conversation centered on affordability and housing challenges. Local activist Delories Butts asked why the community can't help homeless people, while other residents shared reasons they love living in Belle Glade. Lavita Holmes, executive director of Glades Lives Matter, highlighted the organization's ambassadorship program, which selects three students from every school to mentor throughout the year. Holmes said the program holds students civically responsible for attending school board meetings, commission meetings, and staying informed about their communities.

The meetup also featured announcements about upcoming events. Codi Snead announced the first Juneteenth pageant in the county's history, currently featuring eight contestants from kindergarten through 5th grade. The Let's Hear It events aim to capture the real stories that define communities. Residents unable to attend the monthly meetups can share their stories and concerns by emailing LetsHearIt@wptv.com.

cards.headline: Friends mourn 14-year-old struck by speeding driver in Boynton Beach
cards.teaser: Friends of Christopher Cetoute are mourning the loss of the 14-year-old, who was fatally struck by a speeding driver Friday night along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach.
cards.body:
Friends of 14-year-old Christopher Cetoute are mourning his death after he was struck by a speeding driver Friday night along the 4600 block of North Congress Avenue in Boynton Beach. According to Boynton Beach Police, Christopher was crossing the roadway going eastbound when he was struck by a 35-year-old driver traveling southbound. Police believe speeding played a factor in the crash. Christopher was not crossing at a crosswalk and was pronounced dead on scene. A memorial of flowers, a poster and a balloon now stands near the scene.

Abrionna Lang, a close friend, remembered Christopher as someone who attended Congress Middle School and loved playing basketball and track. "Loyal, hilarious, determined, caring, a sweet person. He was always easy to get close to," Lang said. She described learning of his death, saying "At first I didn't believe it until I'd seen a lot of stuff and then I just started crying. Like I was crying for the whole day." The tragedy resonated with nearby resident Caurline Robinson, who lost her 5-year-old great-grandchild to a speeding driver in 2021. Robinson said she has witnessed at least 7 crashes along Congress Avenue in the last 8 years and is calling for safety enhancements. No charges have been filed against the driver. A vigil will be held in Christopher's honor Friday at 7pm at the memorial site on North Congress Avenue.
